title: Every Promotion Is a Subtraction
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain challenges the assumption that a promotion is purely additive, arguing instead that every promotion requires a corresponding subtraction of the exact strengths that earned it, and that failing to let go of those strengths deliberately can eventually undermine the person in the new role. His central case study is the technically excellent engineer promoted to manager who keeps solving every hard problem personally, which feels like diligence but actually deprives the team of the growth opportunities that come from struggling with problems themselves. Jain's sharpest observation is that this failure to subtract is unusually hard to detect because it disguises itself as virtue: leaders tell themselves they're maintaining high standards or staying close to the work, when in fact those very habits are what's now holding their team back. He connects this to a structural problem of seniority — the higher a leader climbs, the more colleagues start 'managing up' rather than giving honest feedback, meaning the people with the most power get the least accurate information about what they need to change. The piece closes with a concrete self-diagnostic checklist, including the piercing question of whether whatever a leader complains their team isn't doing is 'usually the exact thing you haven't stopped doing for them.'
points: Jain's core mechanism — that promotion-earning strengths become identity-protecting habits disguised as virtues ('I hold the bar high') — explains why leaders often can't self-diagnose the problem: the behavior feels principled, not limiting.

The observation that 'the people with the most power and authority get the least honest feedback about the thing that they need to hear' identifies a structural, seniority-driven feedback failure that compounds the subtraction problem over time.

The diagnostic reframe — 'whatever you complain about your team not doing is usually the exact thing you haven't stopped doing for them' — gives leaders an immediately actionable self-test rather than an abstract principle to remember.
quotes: We typically think of a promotion as an addition. After all, a promotion usually comes with a bigger title, a larger team or scope, and more authority. But in this piece I'm going to argue that promotions actually take something away from you, and for good reason.
you ended up depriving your team members of the growth and learning opportunities, instead of creating more of them.
This is really hard to detect, because your behavior typically shows up as a "virtue".
The people with the most power and authority get the least honest feedback about the thing that they need to hear.
If you can't let go of something that you used to do yourself, even after you got promoted, that's a sign that you're holding on to the old identity.
Whatever you complain about your team not doing is usually the exact thing you haven't stopped doing for them.
If you got promoted again tomorrow, what would you keep doing out of habit that the new role wouldn't actually need?
